posts.title: Foundations
posts.html:
Every other decision on the platform is downstream of the objects you drew on day one. A field type chosen badly is a migration later; a relationship chosen badly is a rebuild.

What this module covers

The data model, the field types worth arguing about, and the two relationship kinds that look alike in the setup menu and behave nothing alike in practice.
posts.custom_excerpt: The data model first: everything else on the platform is a consequence of it.

posts.title: Standard vs custom objects
posts.html:
Account, Contact, Opportunity and Case arrive with fields, layouts, reports and — the part people forget — behaviour that other features assume.

When to add your own

Add a custom object when the thing you are modelling is genuinely not one of the standard ones. "It is a bit like an Opportunity" usually means you want an Opportunity with a record type.

The cost of getting it wrong

A custom object that duplicates a standard one splits your reporting in half and doubles the automation you maintain. Both halves drift, and the day someone asks which number is right, neither is.
posts.custom_excerpt: What ships with the org, what you add, and why the boundary matters.

posts.title: Field types, and the three you will regret
posts.html:
Free text is the easy answer and the expensive one. Six months in you have "UK", "U.K." and a blank, and no report can group them.

Derive what can be derived

A stored number is a number someone has to remember to update. The moment two places disagree, the field stops being trusted at all.

Dates beat checkboxes

"Is approved" answers less than "approved on", and costs the same. A date gives you the boolean for free — it is either null or it is not — plus every question about when and how long.
posts.custom_excerpt: Picking a field type is a one-way door more often than it looks.

posts.title: Lookup vs master-detail
posts.html:
Master-detail means the detail record belongs to its master: delete the master and the details go with it. A lookup is a reference — delete the target and the field empties.

Sharing follows the master

A detail record inherits its master’s sharing, so you cannot grant access to a detail without access to its parent. That is either exactly what you want or a wall you will argue with for a week.

Roll-up summaries

Only master-detail gives you roll-up summary fields. If you know you need a count or a sum on the parent, the relationship decision is already made.
posts.custom_excerpt: Two relationships that look alike and behave nothing alike.

posts.title: Security and access
posts.html:
Salesforce answers access in two halves: what a user can do to an object, and which records of it they can see. Profiles and permission sets answer the first; the role hierarchy and sharing rules answer the second.

Why the order matters

Almost every access bug is someone solving one half with the other half’s tool.
posts.custom_excerpt: Profiles, permission sets, roles and sharing — in that order, because each only makes sense given the last.

posts.title: Profiles vs permission sets
posts.html:
A profile is the baseline every user of that kind gets, and a user has exactly one. It is the wrong place for anything only some of them need.

The grant

A permission set adds on top, and a user can have any number. Anything optional, temporary, or true of a person rather than a role belongs in one.

The rule of thumb

If you are about to clone a profile, stop: you want the original plus a permission set naming the difference. The name of that difference is the name of the permission set.
posts.custom_excerpt: One is a floor, the other is a grant.

posts.title: The role hierarchy
posts.html:
The role hierarchy grants record access upward: someone above you can see the records you can see. That is its whole job.

Why copying the org chart hurts

An org chart is deep, because management is. A role hierarchy that deep gives half the company visibility of everything, and every level is access you did not deliberately grant.

Build it from access, not titles

Ask who legitimately needs to see whose records, and draw the shallowest tree that answers it. Three levels covers most organisations.
posts.custom_excerpt: It is not your org chart.

posts.title: Org-wide defaults, and why you start private
posts.html:
Org-wide defaults set the most restrictive access anyone has. Everything else — hierarchy, sharing rules, manual shares — only ever opens access up. Nothing narrows it again.

Start private

Because access only widens, starting private makes every grant afterwards deliberate and traceable. Starting public means the only way to take access away is to change the default later, and by then nobody knows who relied on it.

The conversation this causes

Someone will say it is easier to open everything and lock down later. It is easier exactly once, and it is a security review finding forever.
posts.custom_excerpt: The one setting that decides whether everything after it opens doors or closes them.

posts.title: Why your Flow is slower than your Apex
posts.html:
The received wisdom is that declarative is slower. It is more accurate to say declarative is slower per element and faster per change.

Where the time actually goes

A record-triggered Flow re-queries in ways Apex would not, because it cannot see the whole transaction the way you can. Most of the gap is queries, not execution.

When to reach for code

Loops over large collections, anything needing a bulk pattern you can test, and anything a future admin should not be able to break by dragging a node.

The honest summary

Write the Flow. Measure it. Rewrite the 5% that matters in Apex, and leave the rest alone.
posts.custom_excerpt: Declarative is slower per element and faster per change. Which matters depends on how often the thing changes.

posts.title: A field-naming convention that survives contact with other people
posts.html:
Naming is the cheapest governance you will ever apply and the first thing dropped under deadline.

The rule

Name the field for what it holds, not for the project that asked for it. Renewal_Date__c outlives Q3_Push_Date__c by years.

Why this page is wide

This post carries the internal tag #hide-sidebar, so it renders full width with no meta column — the same template, one tag different.
posts.custom_excerpt: Name the field for what it holds, not for the project that asked for it.

posts.title: Sharing rules, and the order you fix them in
posts.html:
Org-wide defaults decide the floor; everything after them only ever opens access up. That single fact explains most of the sharing bugs I get sent.

Groups, not roles, in the rule

An owner-based sharing rule written against a public group survives someone moving desks. Written against a role, it quietly stops applying the day they move.

How to check your work

Log in as the user and open a record you believe they should not see. If they can, the hierarchy is granting it rather than your rule — which is a different fix.
posts.custom_excerpt: A teardown of the four levers that decide who sees a record, and why the order you reach for them matters more than any one of them.
